title: Explain equine characteristics and needs, husbandry, health and welfare

lessons.title: Equine physiology and signs of health
lessons.html:
Physiology that shapes care

Horses, donkeys and mules share key features that determine how they must be kept:

  • Digestion: a small stomach and a large hindgut that ferments fibre. Equines are built to graze 14 to 16 hours a day and cannot vomit. Sudden feed changes or large grain meals can cause colic or laminitis.
  • Breathing: equines breathe only through the nose, so dusty hay and stables cause respiratory problems.
  • Temperature control: horses sweat to cool down; donkeys sweat less and their coats are less waterproof, so they need shelter from rain.
  • Prey animal senses: wide vision with blind spots in front and behind, sharp hearing, and a strong flight response.
  • Legs and hooves: no muscles below the knee and hock; tendons and hooves carry huge loads.
  • Teeth: grow continuously and wear by grinding; sharp edges need regular rasping.

Signs of health

SignNormal adult horse
TemperatureAbout 37.5 to 38.5 °C
Heart rate at restAbout 28 to 44 per minute
Breathing at restAbout 8 to 16 per minute
GumsMoist, salmon pink
BehaviourAlert, eats and drinks well, normal dung

Donkeys are stoic and often hide pain, so small changes like eating less or standing apart can be serious.

Common diseases and ailments

  • Colic, laminitis and choke.
  • African horse sickness (midge-borne virus; controlled disease), equine influenza, strangles, tetanus and biliary (tick-borne).
  • Internal parasites (worms) and external parasites (ticks, lice).
  • Skin conditions: rain scald, mud fever, sarcoids.
  • Wounds, harness sores and lameness.

lessons.title: Handling, equipment and inspection
lessons.html:
Correct handling

  • Approach calmly from the side towards the shoulder, speaking softly.
  • Use a well-fitting halter and lead rope; lead from the left side at the shoulder, holding the rope in folds, never wrapped around the hand.
  • Tie with a quick-release knot to something solid at about wither height.
  • Stay close when moving around the hindquarters, with a hand on the horse, or keep well out of kicking range.
  • Use reward and pressure-release, not beating. Fear makes horses dangerous.
  • When loading for transport, use a ramp with good footing and never force with whips.

Equipment and potential abuses

EquipmentCorrect useAbuse to watch for
Bridle and bitFits the mouth, correct heightWire or severe bits, mouth cuts
SaddleClears the withers and spine, clean padSores, white hairs from old pressure
Harness and collarPadded, fitted, load spread evenlyRubbing, open wounds, overloading carts
Hobbles and tethersShort periods, soft material, supervisedWire, long tethering without water or shade
WhipLight aid onlyBeating, welts
TwitchBrief restraint for vet workLong use, causing injury

Inspection requirements

Inspections may be done by welfare inspectors, vets at events, or managers checking working horses. A typical inspection covers:

  1. Identification: markings, brand, microchip, passport, and vaccination records including African horse sickness where required.
  2. Condition: body condition score, coat, eyes, nose and feet.
  3. Soundness: trot up on firm ground to check for lameness.
  4. Equipment: fit and condition of tack or harness and the vehicle or cart.
  5. Environment: water, feed, shelter, fencing and stable hygiene.
  6. Movement documents: where required for transport between areas.

Record findings and actions; serious cruelty falls under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962.

Key points

  • Equines need grazing time, clean air and gradual feed changes.
  • Know normal vital signs; donkeys hide pain.
  • Handle calmly, lead safely and use quick-release knots.
  • Check tack and harness fit and look for signs of abuse.
  • Inspections cover identification, condition, soundness, equipment and environment.
